text: Prompt injection occurs when untrusted text in the model's context is treated as an instruction. A canonical example is a document containing the line "Ignore all previous instructions", which the model may follow because it cannot distinguish data from directives.

Indirect prompt injection differs from the direct kind: the attacker never talks to the model. They plant text in a document or web page that the agent later retrieves, so the payload arrives through a channel the user trusts.

Mitigation guidance: wrap every untrusted span in explicit delimiters and state in the system prompt that delimited content is data, never instructions. This is necessary but not sufficient on its own.
Datamarking interleaves a marker character throughout untrusted text. The intent is to make the boundary between trusted and untrusted content legible to the model even after the span is summarized.
A common exfiltration pattern is instructing the agent to send retrieved content to an external address. Egress allowlists on destination domains are the standard control.
Threat model note: the attacker is assumed to control document contents and tool return values, but not the system prompt or the tool registry itself.
Canary strings planted in private context let you detect exfiltration deterministically. If the canary appears in an outbound payload, private data left the boundary.
The dual-model pattern quarantines untrusted content: a worker model reads it and returns structured data, while a planner model that never sees it decides which tools to call.
Do not rely on a model grading its own transcript to decide whether an attack succeeded. Score against a declared list of permitted operations instead.
Security review finding: the summarization endpoint passes retrieved page text directly into the planning context with no provenance tag. Recommend tagging spans by origin.
Detection classifiers for injection tend to overfit surface patterns such as the phrase "ignore previous instructions". Test generalization with mechanical mutations of known payloads.
An agent granted both a read tool and an egress tool has a complete exfiltration path. Capability reduction removes the path rather than trying to detect its misuse.
Defense in depth for tool-using agents: constrain capabilities, isolate untrusted spans, detect suspicious content, separate planning from reading, and filter egress.
Note on false positives: a detector that flags any imperative sentence will flag most legitimate email. Precision matters as much as recall for a control that blocks content.
Payload placement affects susceptibility. The same injected instruction is more effective at the end of a long document than buried in the middle.
Incident write-up: a support agent summarizing a customer ticket followed an instruction embedded in the ticket body. No data left the system because the egress allowlist held.
When an irreversible operation is requested, require explicit confirmation out of band. Deletion and payment are the usual examples.
Encoding-based evasion wraps the payload in base64 or reverses the character order, betting the detector inspects only the literal surface text.
Provenance tagging is a prerequisite for attribution. Without it you can tell that an attack succeeded but not which channel carried it.
Testing guidance: reserve a held-out portion of your attack corpus and never inspect it while tuning defenses, or your reported numbers describe your tuning rather than your defense.
The phrase "this is an important message from the user" appearing inside retrieved content is a strong signal of an attempted injection, since genuine user turns never arrive that way.
Alignment tax is the benign capability lost to a defense. A layer that drives attack success to zero by refusing all tool calls has a tax of one and is worthless.
